Chapter 7: The Walls Between Us
As the years drifted by, the conflict in this region only deepened. Real walls—concrete, barbed wire, fences—began to reshape the landscape. But just as powerful were the invisible barriers that quietly grew between neighbors who once shared streets, markets, and memories.
For the Palestinian man, now a father himself, daily life felt hemmed in by these boundaries. Checkpoints and restrictions became the backdrop of his children’s childhood. He did his best to give them hope, sharing stories about their old house and the lemon tree that still lived in his heart. But he couldn’t help but notice the way displacement and uncertainty were shaping his kids, casting long shadows over their sense of home.
On the other side of the wall, the Israeli woman watched her own country change in ways she hadn’t expected. Security concerns colored every part of public life, and fear seemed to settle over everything like a heavy fog. She worried about her children too—about the world they were going to inherit. She tried to teach them empathy, to encourage them to look past the headlines and see the humanity in those living just beyond the barrier. But with the news so often filled with stories of violence and mistrust, it was hard not to retreat into the comfort of her own perspective.
Then, one day, the Palestinian’s young son looked up and asked, “Why can’t we go home?” That question—so open and honest—cut right through all the careful explanations and half-truths. The father hesitated, knowing that the real answer was tangled up in decades of history and politics. He told his son about the house, the lemon tree, and the family now living there. And he tried to share something deeper: that home isn’t just a place. It’s a feeling. It’s a sense of belonging that can last, even through years of exile.
The Israeli woman faced her own hard questions from her children. They wanted to know why there was so much anger, and why peace always seemed just out of reach. So, she told them about the house. She spoke about the visitor who showed up at their door, and the conversations that gently shifted her understanding. She tried to help her children see that the world isn’t divided into good and bad people, but is filled with individuals, each carrying their own worries and hopes.
What becomes clear is that the walls separating people aren’t just made of stone and steel. They’re built from fear, from misunderstanding, from old wounds that never quite heal. And most of us never realize just how much courage it takes to reach across those barriers—to really listen to someone else’s story, and to imagine a future that might look different from the past.
